draft.title: Inner peace and world peace
card: Inner peace is a calm and settled state of mind and heart. Many religions teach that a person can work towards it.
Paths to inner peace include prayer, meditation, worship and reflection on sacred texts. Each tradition has its own practices and its own reasons for them.
Many religions see inner peace as a basis for peace between people. A person who is calm and free of anger is more likely to treat others with patience and respect.
World peace is peace between individuals, communities and nations. Religions often teach that it grows from people changing themselves first, and that this can then shape how they act towards others.
draft.remember: Many religions teach that peace begins within a person and can then shape how people treat each other.

a.q: Why do many religions teach practices such as prayer and meditation as part of building peace in the world?
opts: They calm a person, which can shape how they treat others
They remove the need for laws between nations
They guarantee that wars will stop once enough people pray
They replace relationships with other people as a focus
a.why: Many religions see a settled mind as the basis for patient and respectful action towards others. The option about guaranteeing an end to wars is wrong because the card says inner peace is a basis, which can shape behaviour, not a guarantee.
a.clue: Think about what a calm person is more likely to do.

b.q: Layla is a member of a faith community. She meditates each morning and finds she argues less with her family and neighbours. Which idea does her experience best show?
opts: Inner peace can be a basis for peace between people
Inner peace and world peace are two unrelated ideas
World peace must be reached before inner peace
Meditation is only a private act with no effect on others
b.why: Layla's calmer state leads to fewer arguments, which matches the idea that inner peace can be a basis for peace between people. The option that puts world peace first is tempting but reverses the order of the idea: it is taught as growing from the person outwards.
b.clue: Look at what changed in Layla first, and what followed.

a.best: They calm a person, which can shape how they treat others

b.best: Inner peace can be a basis for peace between people

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('can shape'), while every distractor is an absolute claim ('guarantee', 'remove the need', 'replace'). A student could pick it by spotting the qualifier. The clue ('what a calm person is more likely to do') also nearly states the answer.

The distractors use 'only' and 'must', where the card says 'can'. Only the right option carries the card's 'can' qualifier, and it echoes the remember line almost word for word, so it stands out without the student knowing the idea.

proposal.title: Inner peace and world peace
card: Inner peace is a calm and settled state of mind and heart. Many religions teach that a person can work towards it.
Paths to inner peace include prayer, meditation, worship and reflection on sacred texts. Each tradition has its own practices and its own reasons for them.

World peace is peace between individuals, communities and nations. Religions often teach that it grows from people changing themselves first, and that this can then shape how they act towards others.
proposal.remember: Many religions teach that peace begins within a person and can then shape how people treat each other.

a.q: Sam says meditation is a private practice with nothing to do with world peace. How would many religions respond?
opts: A calm mind helps a person treat others with respect
Peace between nations depends on treaties, not people
Meditation matters for monks and nuns, not for others
Sam is right, as inner peace is a separate private goal
a.why: Many religions see inner peace as a basis for peace between people, because a calm person is more likely to act with patience and respect. Agreeing with Sam is tempting, but it treats inner peace as cut off from others, which is the link these religions reject.
a.clue: Consider how religions connect a person's mind to their actions.

b.q: Layla is a member of a faith community. She meditates each morning and finds she argues less with her family and neighbours. Which idea does her experience best show?
opts: Change within a person flows outward to their relationships
Calm relationships come first and bring about inner peace
Meditation keeps a person's calm apart from family life
Meditation is a way to avoid having to deal with others
b.why: Layla changed herself first through meditation, and her dealings with others then became calmer. The option that puts calm relationships first is tempting, but it reverses the order: religions teach that peace grows from the person outwards.
b.clue: Look at what changed in Layla first, and what followed.
